title: Weaving in ends
subtitle: Finishing the cut tails so they stay put
excerpt: Every crochet piece leaves cut tails where you started, changed colour, or fastened off. Weaving them in cleanly is what makes a piece look finished and stops it coming undone in the wash. This covers the method and how to lock a tail so it holds.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the closing notes on fastening off and securing the ends of a finished piece, supported by the general needlework finishing principles in the same volume. Public domain via Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: Threading each leftover yarn tail through the back of the fabric so it is hidden and held, then trimming it. The standard way to finish crochet.
A blunt large-eyed needle used to weave in ends. Its blunt tip slides between yarn strands without splitting them.
Cutting the yarn and pulling the tail through the last loop to lock the work so it cannot unravel before the tail is woven in.

content.text: Every piece leaves cut tails: one where you began, one each time you changed colour or ball, and one where you
fasten off
at the end.
Weaving in ends
hides those tails in the back of the fabric and locks them so the work holds together through use and washing. It is the quiet step that separates a finished piece from a homemade-looking one.
What you need
The finished piece with its tails left at least 10 cm long.
One tapestry needle with an eye big enough for your yarn.
Sharp scissors for trimming.
How to do it
Thread one tail onto the
tapestry needle
Weave the needle through the back loops of three or four stitches, following the line of the fabric.
Turn and weave back through two or three stitches in the opposite direction. This change of direction is what locks the tail.
Give the fabric a gentle stretch so the woven tail settles into the stitches.
Trim the tail close to the surface, leaving a few millimetres so it does not pop back out.
You will know a tail is secure when a firm tug does not pull it loose and the woven line does not show on the front. After a wash the ends should still be invisible and holding.
Common mistakes
Weaving in a straight line only. Without the change of direction the tail slides out with use. Always double back.
Cutting the tail flush. Trim close but leave a few millimetres, or the end works its way to the front.
Leaving tails too short to thread. Cut at least 10 cm when you fasten off, more on slippery yarn.
When to use it

Weave in ends as the final step of every project, and whenever you change colour or join a new ball mid-piece. On a granny square that means four tails per square; on a colourful blanket it can mean dozens. Doing them as you go, rather than saving them all for the end, keeps the job from becoming a chore.
